11.0.0.en: 1- "In the Lord put I my trust: how say ye to my soul, Flee as a bird to your mountain?"

11.0.1.en: 1- David's friends advised him to flee from the face of Saul, who was pursuing him, lest he kill him, and perhaps during that time he was still in Saul's service; but he refused, relying on God who protects him.

11.0.2.en: 2- The meaning intended by the word "flee" in the Hebrew original is confusion and alarm, that is, flight in trembling and agitation, like a frightened bird that does not know where to flee. This kind of flight is rejected by the believer who trusts in God, who knows that his refuge is God.

11.0.3.en: 3- Flight is to be from evil and sin and all the snares of Satan, but at the same time a person accepts suffering and the bearing of the cross, as the martyrs endured. So David endured the heavy commands and demands of Saul, such as killing a hundred Philistines to present them as a dowry for marrying Saul's daughter, but he did not flee out of fear of Saul.

11.0.4.en: 4- Flight is useful when it is aimed at not being hindered from life with God, like Christ's flight from the face of Herod, and as David himself fled from the face of Saul, and endured his pursuit and was not hindered from his goal, which is life with God, by clashing with Saul, but he was patient until Saul died in the war, as a divine punishment for him.

11.0.5.en: 5- Although mountains are a symbol of strength and material steadfastness, the believer does not flee to them, but to God, who is the true mountain and the fortified refuge; a person must not rely on the material powers in the world, but on God.

11.0.6.en: 6- David answered at once that the solution is trust in God, and he did not even discuss the idea of fleeing out of fear of the wicked, because his faith is firm.

11.0.7.en: 7- David's friends said to him, "Flee," because they meant David and those with him, that is, the soldiers who followed him. But his trust in God caused Saul to fall into his hand twice, and David forgave him and did not kill him (1 Sam 24:4-11, 1 Sam 26:9-11).

11.1.0.en: 2- "For, lo, the wicked bend their bow, they make ready their arrow upon the string, that they may privily shoot at the upright in heart."

11.1.1.en: Make ready their arrow upon the string: the notch of the arrow is its end, and to fit the arrow means to place its end on the string, in readiness to release it.

11.1.2.en: Privily: in the darkness of the night.

11.1.3.en: 1- David's friends based their advice to him to flee on the fact that the wicked had prepared their weapons to do away with him, namely arrows.

11.1.4.en: 2- Arrows are mostly used to hunt people and kill them when they are not prepared, that is, by trickery and deceit, and this shows the evil of the wicked.

11.1.5.en: 3- Bending the bow and fitting the arrow means complete readiness to harm David, but they had not yet shot the arrows; this shows how near evil was to David, and therefore it was necessary for him to flee quickly.

11.1.6.en: 4- David replies to his friends with three things:

11.1.7.en: a - that he has trusted in God, as mentioned in (v. 1), and therefore he is not shaken by the enemies.

11.1.8.en: b - that his enemies are wicked, and God does not answer or support the wicked, but is against them, so they therefore have no real power.

11.1.9.en: c - he is among the upright in heart, who are under God's protection, so the wicked cannot harm him.

11.1.10.en: 5- The cruelty of the wicked appears in that they try to kill him secretly, that is, in the darkness; they are not open enemies, but deceivers.

11.1.11.en: 6- These wicked people may be the heretics, who twist the word of God, and who are symbolized by the arrows that strike in the darkness, and also the time of persecution; that is, heretics and the wicked in general seize the opportunity of the persecution of the children of God to harm them. This is the goal of Satan, to destroy the children of God, but God does not allow him.

11.2.0.en: 3- "If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?" (literally: if the pillars are overturned, what does the righteous do?)

11.2.1.en: 1- David's friends continue their advice to him: if the pillars fall, what will be the condition of the righteous man? And what is meant by the pillars is:

11.2.2.en: a - The righteous kings and rulers who fear God.

11.2.3.en: b - The principles and values prevailing in society.

11.2.4.en: c - Respect for the spiritual leaders, such as the prophets of the Old Testament, or the bishops and priests in the Church.

11.2.5.en: d - The word of God and the teachings of the Church.

11.2.6.en: 2- The fall of the pillars means the following:

11.2.7.en: a - The death of important persons in the Church; as happened in the Old Testament when Saul killed the priests dwelling in the city of Nob (1 Sam 22:17-19). What would David the righteous do without priests?

11.2.8.en: b - Their deviation from God and their preoccupation with the world.

11.2.9.en: c - Their falling into innovations and heresies.

11.2.10.en: 3- The righteous man who is meant is:

11.2.11.en: a - David the prophet, in whose time King Saul and many of the rulers, teachers and people became corrupt, and they are symbolized by the pillars.

11.2.12.en: b - Christ our Lord, who sees that His teachings have been neglected, the righteous have fallen and the people of innovations have spread; what does He do, except judge them on the last day.

11.2.13.en: c - Any person who lives in godliness, when he sees the pillars falling, has nothing before him except to take refuge in God and be sheltered in Him, so that He establishes him in the faith to the end.

11.2.14.en: Do not be troubled in afflictions, for they are temporary; hold fast to your faith, trusting in God, confident that the end of evil is destruction, and that God will not leave you, but will support you and comfort you and gladden your heart during the affliction, and then you will enjoy complete joy in heaven.

11.3.s.en: (2) The care of the righteous and the vengeance on the wicked

11.3.0.en: 4- "The Lord is in his holy temple, the Lord's throne is in heaven: his eyes behold, his eyelids try, the children of men."

11.3.1.en: 1- Since the pillars had fallen, and the wicked had aimed their arrows at David, and his friends had advised him to flee like a bird, David had nothing before him except to take refuge in God, the strong and just, who cares for him and keeps him, so he looks to God in His holy temple and in His heaven.

11.3.2.en: 2- What is meant by the holy temple of God is:

11.3.3.en: a - The tabernacle of meeting, or, in the spirit of prophecy, the Church of the New Testament.

11.3.4.en: b - God in His heavenly Kingdom.

11.3.5.en: c - The just God, who dwells in heaven, who will judge all on the Day of Judgment.

11.3.6.en: d - The souls of God's children, where He works in them, so that they become a light to the world and condemn the evil of the wicked.

11.3.7.en: 3- David looked to the Lord, whose throne is in heaven, to raise his thoughts, words and deeds to heaven and live spiritually, and to keep away from the enemy, Satan, who wants to bring him down to earthly things and make him live carnally. By this David wants to live in the light of heaven, while the enemy wants to fight him with darkness, as in (v. 2).

11.3.8.en: 4- By David's looking to heaven to see the justice of God, he is not troubled by the spread of injustice on earth, and the persecution of the upright in heart and the righteous by the wicked, as in (vv. 2, 3). And by his looking to heaven he flees to God with faith and strength and not in trembling to the mountains like a bird, as his companions advised him (v. 1).

11.3.9.en: 5- When the eyes of God look on mankind, this means:

11.3.10.en: a - Care and providence for His righteous children.

11.3.11.en: b - Condemnation of the wicked, with whom He is patient, but He destroys them if they continue in their disobedience.

11.3.12.en: 6- The eyelids try mankind; because the eyelids of God are a symbol of:

11.3.13.en: a - When God opens His eyelids He sees with His eyes, His love and His care the life of His children, then He closes His eyes to the wicked, because they have left Him and neglected life with Him and insisted on evil, although He called them many times, so He abandons them, perhaps they will grow weary of their evils and return to Him.

11.3.14.en: b - When God opens His eyelids He declares His judgments to mankind, and at other times He closes His eyelids, that is, His judgments are hidden, not seen by mankind, but understood only by the righteous, when they lift up prayers to Him.

11.3.15.en: c - When God opens His eyelids He tests mankind with success, to see how thankful they are to Him, and when He closes His eyelids He tests them with failure and hardship, to see how steadfast they are in the faith.

11.3.16.en: 7- The eyelids of God try the children of Adam, that is, all mankind, so that the righteous may be proved and the wicked may perish.

11.4.0.en: 5- "The Lord trieth the righteous: but the wicked and him that loveth violence his soul hateth."

11.4.1.en: 1- God cares for His righteous children so as to purify them from every evil that clings to them from the world, which is full of evil, so He tests them with afflictions until they return to Him, so that their faith is established and they keep away from everything that angers God.

11.4.2.en: 2- God abandons the wicked because of their insistence on evil, and then they lose their peace and become distressed with themselves, and God allows this, perhaps they will return to Him, when they taste the results of their sins and see the peace of the righteous, so they are pricked in their hearts and repent.

11.4.3.en: 3- The continuance of the wicked and those who love injustice in their sins will lead them to eternal destruction, and in the torment their souls will hate them; because they brought this destruction upon themselves.

11.5.0.en: 6- "Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone, and a wind of poison shall be the portion of their cup."

11.5.1.en: 1- The wicked, who by their evil deeds harm themselves, God leaves to the torment of their consciences throughout their lives, perhaps they will repent, and He allows them to fall into the snares of the evil they loved, whether the snares of evil lusts, or innovations and heresies. And if they do not return to God, nothing awaits them but divine punishment on the Day of Judgment. God allows them to fall into the snares, just as they also set snares for the righteous, but God delivered the righteous from them, whereas the wicked, because of their distance from God, fell into these snares and did not rise.

11.5.2.en: 2- These snares which God allows are so many that He likens them to rain, and in this God gives the wicked many opportunities to repent.

11.5.3.en: 3- If the wicked do not return to God they will deserve eternal torment, which is expressed here by fire and brimstone, and the severity of this fire cannot be measured by the fire we know; because it burns spirits and continues for ever. As for the brimstone, it is an expression of the speed of burning and also of the foul smell, and it is like the foul smell of sin, and all this shows the horror of eternal torment. God expressed this when He burned Sodom and Gomorrah with fire and brimstone, to be a lesson to all the wicked and a likeness of what will happen in the eternal torment.

11.5.4.en: 4- By wind is meant spirits, and as for poison, it is known to be deadly; so God allows the spirits of the wicked to go astray and lead them to destruction, because they reject God, and they also submit to the spirits of the demons and their thoughts, which lead to eternal torment.

11.5.5.en: 5- All these preceding punishments are the portion of the wicked, and He has expressed their portion by the cup, that is, the cup of God's wrath which they deserve. And the cups differ in capacity, that is, each wicked man receives his portion and the cup of divine wrath that he deserves according to his sins, not only on this earth but in eternity; for hell has degrees of torment, according to the evil of each one.

11.6.0.en: 7- "For the righteous Lord loveth righteousness; his countenance doth behold the upright."

11.6.1.en: 1- David begins the psalm with trust in God and ends it with looking to the just God; God is the beginning and the end, and therefore faith and steadfastness in Him is life on this earth and for ever.

11.6.2.en: 2- If the upright meet afflictions in life and injustice from the wicked, God supports them and comforts them in the afflictions by their seeing God, as happened with the three young men in the fiery furnace, and as happens every day with the children of God who seek Him in affliction.

11.6.3.en: 3- God must compensate the upright for their endurance of sufferings in this life, in eternal life, by shining upon them with His face, and they enjoy Him for ever. This is the perfection of justice.

11.6.4.en: Seek God in every affliction that meets you, confident that He is beside you and is able to comfort you with a joy that makes you forget the pains, so that you are strengthened, and even become an example to those around you and draw them to life with God.

11.6.5.en: The cry of the poor and God's intervention. For the choir director, on the "Sheminith." A psalm of David. "Help, Lord, for the godly man ceaseth"... (v. 1). Introduction:

11.6.6.en: 1- Its writer: David, and he used to sing it through a group that had a director, or leader.

11.6.7.en: 2- The occasion on which this psalm was said:

11.6.9.en: a - When David was serving Saul and there were rumors from Saul's assistants, who flattered him and spoke evil words against David, David cried out to God to rescue him and support him.

11.6.10.en: b - When the Philistines attacked the city of Keilah and plundered it, David cried out to God and asked for His guidance, and He told him to fight the Philistines and deliver Keilah. This was during his flight from Saul (1 Sam 23:1-6).

11.6.11.en: 3- In the title of this psalm it says "on the Sheminith" (literally: on the octave), which is one of the degrees of the voice, on which this psalm is chanted.

11.6.12.en: 4- In the Septuagint translation this psalm is titled with the words "to the end" or "for completion", which means that God's intervention and His rescue of the poor continue throughout the days, that is, throughout the life of mankind.

11.6.13.en: 5- Also in the Septuagint translation this psalm is titled with the words "for the eighth" or "concerning the eighth", and this means that the words of the wicked come to nothing, while the righteous are those who remain with God to the eighth, which is a symbol of eternity, that is, the righteous remain with God for ever, while the wicked go to hell.

11.6.14.en: 6- We find a relationship between Psalms 9, 10, 11, 12 and also Psalm 14, for all of them speak about the words and deeds of the wicked and God's intervention to rescue His poor children; they are suitable for times of affliction and injustice, so the children of God repeat these psalms to receive God's help.

11.6.15.en: 7- This psalm is in the prayer of Prime in the Agpeya, and its number differs, taking number 11 in the Agpeya because Psalms 9 and 10 are joined into one psalm in the Septuagint translation from which the Agpeya was taken.
